name: Spill and plume
description: Oil and hazardous release response: notifications, unified command, trajectory and sensitive-area decisions, booming and countermeasures, with the ICS forms and field reports a spill management team uses, and support for the PREP exercise record.
outsideParties: Coast Guard Sector duty officer and Captain of the Port
Federal On-Scene Coordinator (Coast Guard or EPA)
state environmental agency and state On-Scene Coordinator
oil spill removal organization duty manager

advisorRoles.name: Scientific Support Coordinator
advisorRoles.description: Explains the trajectory, its uncertainty, weathering and the trade-offs of each countermeasure; never decides.

advisorRoles.name: Wildlife Branch Director
advisorRoles.description: Reports animal counts and permit status; explains what hazing and capture can and cannot do.

advisorRoles.name: Environmental Unit Leader
advisorRoles.description: Ranks sensitive areas and resources at risk from the area plan and the ESI maps.

advisorRoles.name: OSRO Duty Manager
advisorRoles.description: Says what equipment and crews can reach which site and when.

glossary.definition: Qualified Individual: the person with authority to activate the plan and commit resources.
Incident (older: spill) Management Team: the responsible party's trained response team.
Federal On-Scene Coordinator (Coast Guard or EPA); decides countermeasures with the Regional Response Team.
Federal, state and responsible party commanders deciding objectives together.
Worst case discharge: a vessel's entire cargo in adverse weather; a facility's or pipeline segment's plan volume.
Area Contingency Plan: sensitive areas, strategies and preauthorizations for one area.
Environmental Sensitivity Index: shoreline types and resources ranked by sensitivity.
Shoreline Cleanup Assessment Technique: segment surveys of oiling and treatment.
National Response Center: the 24-hour reporting point. A call to it is a report, not a request.

productConventions: Notification order: finder, then the Qualified Individual, then the responsible party reports to the NRC and the state, and activates the OSRO.
Use one volume unit per document (barrels, gallons or cubic meters); show estimates with their basis.
A trajectory gives a time window per site with the model run time, not one time.
A countermeasure is a request, then a decision by the FOSC with conditions and time.
Boom plans give site, length, type, anchoring, who deploys and when.
Wildlife counts: oiled live, oiled dead, hazed, in rehabilitation, released.
realismRules: The responsible party calls the NRC; the NRC sends no responders and approves nothing.
Only the FOSC approves dispersant, a chemical agent or a burn.
A state agency or local authority closes a fishery or beach; a utility closes its intake; the responsible party does not.
Never mix barrels, gallons and cubic meters in one document.
Call a release a worst case discharge only if the plan's scenario says so.
Boom fails in currents above about 1 knot across it or in steep waves.
Dispersant and burn need weathering, wind and distance-from-shore criteria; state them.
Use a fictional responsible party and 555-01xx phone numbers; real geography is fine.
